claim: Private, subjective beliefs about uncertainty have idiosyncratic computational and neural substrates.
source: Private, subjective beliefs about uncertainty have been found to have idiosyncratic computational and neural substrates yet, humans share such beliefs seamlessly and cooperate successfully.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature establishing inter-individual diversity in uncertainty representations.

claim: Humans share subjective beliefs about uncertainty seamlessly and cooperate successfully.
source: Private, subjective beliefs about uncertainty have been found to have idiosyncratic computational and neural substrates yet, humans share such beliefs seamlessly and cooperate successfully.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact in the abstract, drawing on general knowledge about human cooperation.

claim: Shared (reported confidence) and subjective (inferred from pupillometry) uncertainty dynamically followed social information.
source: Examining confidence-speed-accuracy trade-off in uncertainty-ridden perceptual decisions under social vs isolated context, we found that shared (i.e. reported confidence) and subjective (inferred from pupillometry) uncertainty dynamically followed social information.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data combining behavioral and pupillometry measurements.

claim: An attractor neural network model incorporating social information as top-down additive input captured the observed behavior.
source: An attractor neural network model incorporating social information as top-down additive input captured the observed behavior and demonstrated the emergence of social alignment in virtual dyadic simulations.
evidence: This is supported by computational modeling results presented in the study.

claim: Social alignment emerged in virtual dyadic simulations of the attractor neural network model.
source: An attractor neural network model incorporating social information as top-down additive input captured the observed behavior and demonstrated the emergence of social alignment in virtual dyadic simulations.
evidence: This is demonstrated through computational simulations shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Social exchange of confidence modulated the neural signature of perceptual evidence accumulation in the central parietal cortex.
source: Electroencephalography showed that social exchange of confidence modulated the neural signature of perceptual evidence accumulation in the central parietal cortex.
evidence: This is a primary finding from EEG data analysis presented in Figure 4.

claim: The same verbal or numerical expression of confidence can have very different meanings for different people in terms of the underlying uncertainty.
source: However, numerous studies have shown that even the same verbal or numerical expression of confidence can have very different meanings for different people in terms of the underlying uncertainty (Ais et al., 2016; Navajas et al., 2017; Fleming et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Similar inter-individual diversity in confidence has been found at the neural level.
source: Similar inter-individual diversity has been found at the neural level (Fleming et al., 2010; Sinanaj et al., 2015; Baird et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to neuroimaging studies.

claim: People manage to cooperate successfully in decision making under uncertainty despite neural and cognitive diversity.
source: Still, people manage to cooperate successfully in decision making under uncertainty (Bahrami et al., 2010; Austen-Smith and Banks, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on joint decision making.

claim: Brain-to-brain coupling could underlie adaptive communication of shared beliefs.
source: A number of studies have provided compelling empirical evidence of brain-to-brain coupling that could underlie adaptive communication of shared beliefs (Silbert et al., 2014; Honey et al., 2012; Hasson et al., 2004; Dikker et al., 2014; Konvalinka et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to brain-to-brain coupling studies.

claim: Studies on brain-to-brain coupling remain mostly observational in nature.
source: These works remain, to date, mostly observational in nature.
evidence: This is an assessment of the existing literature based on the authors' review.

claim: Plausible neuro-computational mechanisms accounting for interpersonal alignment of beliefs from neural populations are still lacking.
source: Plausible neuro-computational mechanism(s) accounting for how interpersonal alignment of beliefs may arise from the firing patterns of decision-related neural populations in the human brain are still lacking (Hasson and Frith, 2016; Wheatley et al., 2019).
evidence: This identifies a gap in the literature supported by citations.

claim: Joint decision makers can surpass their respective individual performance by reducing uncertainty through interaction.
source: By sharing their confidence with others, joint decision makers can surpass their respective individual performance by reducing uncertainty through interaction (Bahrami et al., 2010; Sorkin et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on collective decision making.

claim: During dyadic decision making, interacting partners adjust to one another by matching their own average confidence to that of their partner.
source: Recent works showed that during dyadic decision making, interacting partners adjust to one another by matching their own average confidence to that of their partner (Bang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a specific previous study.

claim: Confidence matching is a good strategy for maximizing joint accuracy under a range of naturalistic conditions.
source: Such confidence matching turns out to be a good strategy for maximizing joint accuracy under a range of naturalistic conditions, e.g., uncertainty about the partner's reliability.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from previous research on confidence matching.

claim: Sequential sampling can provide an optimal strategy for making the best of uncertain, noisy evidence.
source: Theoretical work has shown that sequential sampling can, in principle, provide an optimal strategy for making the best of whatever uncertain, noisy evidence is available to the agent (Heath, 1984).
evidence: This is supported by citation to theoretical work.

claim: Sequential sampling models have had great success in explaining the relationship between decision reaction time and accuracy under a variety of conditions.
source: These models have had great success in explaining the relationship between decision reaction time (RT) and accuracy under a variety of conditions ranging from perceptual (Hanks and Summerfield, 2017; Gold and Shadlen, 2007) to value-based decisions (Ruff and Fehr, 2014) guiding the search for the neuronal mechanisms of evidence accumulation to boundary in rodent and primate brains (Schall, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The relation between RT and accuracy has been extended to a three-way relationship including choice confidence.
source: The relation between RT and accuracy, known as speed-accuracy trade-off, has been recently extended to a three-way relationship in which choice confidence is guided by both RT and probability (or frequency) of correct decision (Pouget et al., 2016; Kiani et al., 2014; Vickers, 1970).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Studies on speed-accuracy-confidence trade-off have focused on decision making in isolated individuals deciding privately.
source: Critically, these studies have all focused on decision making in isolated individuals deciding privately (Wheatley et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an assessment of the literature supported by citation.

claim: Little is known about how computational principles and neuronal mechanisms give rise to socially shared beliefs about uncertainty.
source: Little is known about how these computational principles and neuronal mechanisms can give rise to socially shared beliefs about uncertainty.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge based on literature review.

claim: 12 participants (4 female) were recruited in study 1.
source: We used a discovery-and-replication design to investigate the computational and neurobiological substrates of confidence matching in two separate steps: 12 participants (4 female) were recruited in study 1 (discovery) and 15 (5 female, age: 28 (mean) ± Std (7)) in study 2 (replication, second study was pre-registered: https://osf.io/5zces).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental design.

claim: 15 participants (5 female, age: 28 (mean) ± Std (7)) were recruited in study 2.
source: We used a discovery-and-replication design to investigate the computational and neurobiological substrates of confidence matching in two separate steps: 12 participants (4 female) were recruited in study 1 (discovery) and 15 (5 female, age: 28 (mean) ± Std (7)) in study 2 (replication, second study was pre-registered: https://osf.io/5zces).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental design.

claim: Study 2 was pre-registered at https://osf.io/5zces.
source: We used a discovery-and-replication design to investigate the computational and neurobiological substrates of confidence matching in two separate steps: 12 participants (4 female) were recruited in study 1 (discovery) and 15 (5 female, age: 28 (mean) ± Std (7)) in study 2 (replication, second study was pre-registered: https://osf.io/5zces).
evidence: This is a direct statement about study registration.

claim: Participants reported the direction of a random-dot motion stimulus and indicated their confidence while EEG and eye tracking data were recorded simultaneously.
source: In each study, participants reported the direction of a random-dot motion stimulus and indicated their confidence (Figure 1a) while EEG and eye tracking data were recorded, simultaneously.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Participants reached a stable behavioral performance level after an extensive training procedure.
source: After an extensive training procedure (see Materials and methods for the recruitment), participants reached a stable behavioral (accuracy and RT) performance level.
evidence: This describes the training phase of the experiment.

claim: Two experimental sessions were conducted: first a private session (200 trials) then a social session (800 trials for study 1 and 400 for study 2).
source: Then, two experimental sessions were conducted: first a private session (200 trials) in which participants performed the task alone; then a social session (800 trials for study 1 and 400 for study 2) in which they performed the task interactively together with a partner (implied to be another participant in a neighboring lab room).
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: In the social session, participants performed the task interactively together with a partner implied to be another participant in a neighboring lab room.
source: Then, two experimental sessions were conducted: first a private session (200 trials) in which participants performed the task alone; then a social session (800 trials for study 1 and 400 for study 2) in which they performed the task interactively together with a partner (implied to be another participant in a neighboring lab room).
evidence: This describes the social condition of the experiment.

claim: Participants' confidence showed a significant relation to agent confidence in both studies (linear regression p<0.001 for both studies).
source: Participants confidence against agent confidence show a significant relation in both studies (linear regression p<0.001 for both studies).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Under social condition, when participants were paired with high vs low confidence partner, accuracy did not change.
source: Under social condition, when participants were paired with high (magenta) vs low (dark orange) confidence partner, accuracy (top panel) did not change (horizontal lines, 68% confidence interval of bootstrap test with 10,000 repetitions) but confidence (middle panel) and reaction time (RT) (bottom panel) were altered.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Under social condition, when participants were paired with high vs low confidence partner, confidence was altered.
source: Under social condition, when participants were paired with high (magenta) vs low (dark orange) confidence partner, accuracy (top panel) did not change (horizontal lines, 68% confidence interval of bootstrap test with 10,000 repetitions) but confidence (middle panel) and reaction time (RT) (bottom panel) were altered.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Under social condition, when participants were paired with high vs low confidence partner, reaction time was altered.
source: Under social condition, when participants were paired with high (magenta) vs low (dark orange) confidence partner, accuracy (top panel) did not change (horizontal lines, 68% confidence interval of bootstrap test with 10,000 repetitions) but confidence (middle panel) and reaction time (RT) (bottom panel) were altered.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: There was no significant difference in accuracy between high and low confidence partner conditions (p=0.92, p=0.75 for study 1 and 2 respectively, GLMM).
source: We observed that when participants were paired with a high (vs low) confidence partner, there was no significant difference in accuracy between the social conditions (p=0.92, p=0.75 for study 1 and 2 respectively, generalized linear mixed model [GLMM], see Supplementary materials for details of the analysis [Table 1], Figure 1c top-left panel)
evidence: This is a statistical result from GLMM analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Confidence was significantly higher in HCA vs LCA condition (p<0.001 for both studies, GLMM).
source: confidence, however, was significantly higher (p<0.001 for both studies, Table 1, Figure 1c middle panel)
evidence: This is a statistical result from GLMM analysis of behavioral data.

claim: RTs were significantly faster in HCA vs LCA condition (p<0.001 for both studies, GLMM).
source: RTs were significantly faster (p<0.001 for both, Table 1, Figure 1c bottom panel) in the HCA vs LCA.
evidence: This is a statistical result from GLMM analysis of behavioral data.

claim: The pattern of dissociations of speed and confidence from accuracy is non-trivial because standard sequential sampling models would predict that a change in confidence should be reflected in change in accuracy.
source: This pattern of dissociations of speed and confidence from accuracy is non-trivial because the expectations of the standard sequential sampling models would be that a change in confidence should be reflected in change in accuracy (Pouget et al., 2016; Sanders et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on theoretical expectations from cited models.

claim: Several studies have established a link between state of uncertainty and baseline variations in pupil size.
source: Several studies have recently established a link between state of uncertainty and baseline (i.e. non-luminance mediated) variations in pupil size (Bang et al., 2017; Wei and Wang, 2015; Nassar et al., 2012; Eldar et al., 2013; Murphy et al., 2014; Urai et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: During the inter-trial interval, pupil size was larger in the blocks where participants were paired with LCA vs HCA (GLMM analysis, p<0.01 and p<0.001 for study 1 and 2 respectively).
source: We found that during the inter-trial interval (ITI), pupil size was larger in the blocks where participants were paired with LCA (vs HCA) (Figure 2, GLMM analysis, p<0.01 and p<0.001 for study 1 and 2 respectively, see Supplementary materials for details of the analysis; Table 2).
evidence: This is a statistical result from pupillometry data analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Pupil dilation has been linked to mental effort.
source: It is important to bear in mind that pupil dilation has been linked to other factors such as mental effort (Lee and Daunizeau, 2021), level of surprise (Kloosterman et al., 2015), and arousal level (Murphy et al., 2014) as well.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Pupil dilation has been linked to level of surprise.
source: It is important to bear in mind that pupil dilation has been linked to other factors such as mental effort (Lee and Daunizeau, 2021), level of surprise (Kloosterman et al., 2015), and arousal level (Murphy et al., 2014) as well.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Pupil dilation has been linked to arousal level.
source: It is important to bear in mind that pupil dilation has been linked to other factors such as mental effort (Lee and Daunizeau, 2021), level of surprise (Kloosterman et al., 2015), and arousal level (Murphy et al., 2014) as well.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The patterns of pupil dilation within ITI are consistent with the hypothesis that participants' subjective belief was shaped by interactions with differently confident partners.
source: These caveats notwithstanding, the patterns of pupil dilation within the time period of ITI that are demonstrated and replicated here, are consistent with the hypothesis that participants' subjective belief was shaped by interactions with differently confident partners.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the pupillometry data.

claim: The attractor network model consists of two units simulating the average firing rates of two neural populations involved in information accumulation during perceptual decisions.
source: We employed a previously described attractor network model (Wong and Wang, 2006) which is itself the reduced version of an earlier one (Wang, 2002) inspired by the mean field theory. The model consists of two units simulating the average firing rates of two neural populations involved in information accumulation during perceptual decisions (Figure 3a).
evidence: This describes the computational model used in the study.

claim: In the attractor model, noisy sensory evidence was sequentially accumulated by two competing mechanisms that raced toward a common pre-defined decision boundary while mutually inhibiting each other.
source: Briefly, in this model, noisy sensory evidence was sequentially accumulated by two competing mechanisms (red and blue in Figure 3a left) that raced toward a common pre-defined decision boundary (Figure 3a right) while mutually inhibiting each other.
evidence: This describes the dynamics of the computational model.

claim: Choice was made as soon as one mechanism hits the boundary in the attractor model.
source: Choice was made as soon as one mechanism hits the boundary.
evidence: This describes the decision rule in the computational model.

claim: The attractor model has accounted for numerous observations of perceptual and value-based decision-making behavior and their underlying neuronal substrates in human and non-human primate brain.
source: This model has accounted for numerous observations of perceptual and value-based decision-making behavior and their underlying neuronal substrates in human (Hunt et al., 2012) and non-human primate (Wei and Wang, 2015) brain.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Model confidence was defined as the time-averaged difference between the activity of the winning and losing accumulators during the period of stimulus presentation.
source: Following previous works (Wei and Wang, 2015; Balsdon et al., 2020; Rolls et al., 2010; Atiya et al., 2019) we defined model confidence as the time-averaged difference between the activity of the winning and losing accumulators (corresponding to the shaded gray area between the two accumulator traces in Figure 3a right, for the model simulation see Figure 3—figure supplement 2) during the period of stimulus presentation (from 0 to 500 ms).
evidence: This describes the confidence computation in the model, supported by citations.

claim: Computations of confidence continue after a decision has been made as long as sensory evidence is available.
source: Importantly, this definition of confidence is consistent with recent findings that computations of confidence continue after a decision has been made as long as sensory evidence is available (Ruff and Fehr, 2014; Balsdon et al., 2020; van Kempen et al., 2019; Moran et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent research.

claim: The model's top-down additive input drove both accumulator mechanisms equally and positively.
source: We modeled the social context as a global, top-down additive input (Figure 3a; Wx) in the attractor model. This input drove both accumulator mechanisms equally and positively.
evidence: This describes the modeling approach for social context.

claim: With a positive top-down drive, the winner and the loser traces both rise faster compared to zero top-down drive.
source: The impact of this global top-down input is illustrated in Figure 3a right: with a positive top-down drive (Wx>0), the winner (thick blue) and the loser (thick red) traces both rise faster compared to zero top-down drive (dotted lines).
evidence: This is demonstrated through model simulations shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The surface area between the winning and losing accumulator is larger in the case of positive versus zero top-down input.
source: The model's counterintuitive feature is that the surface area between the winning and losing accumulator is larger in the case of positive (dark gray shading) versus zero (light gray shading) top-down input.
evidence: This is demonstrated through model simulations shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Model simulations show that when 0<Wx, the difference in surface area leads to faster RTs and higher confidence but does not change accuracy.
source: Model simulations show that when 0<Wx, this difference in surface area leads to faster RTs and higher confidence but does not change accuracy because it does not affect the decision boundary.
evidence: This is a result from computational model simulations shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The top-down additive current model was superior to three alternative models in formal model comparison.
source: Formal model comparison showed that our top-down additive current model was superior to all three alternatives (see Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a result from model comparison analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Confidence matching emerged spontaneously when two virtual agents with very different confidence levels in isolated condition were paired with each other as a dyad.
source: Without any fine-tuning of parameters or any other intervention, confidence matching emerged spontaneously when two virtual agents with very different confidence levels in isolated condition (Figure 3d left) were paired with each other as a dyad (Figure 3d right).
evidence: This is a result from virtual dyadic simulations shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Previous works using non-invasive electrophysiological recordings in humans engaged in motion discrimination have identified the signature, accumulate-to-bound neural activity characteristic of evidence accumulation.
source: To identify the neural correlates of interpersonal alignment of belief about uncertainty, we note that previous works using non-invasive electrophysiological recordings in humans engaged in motion discrimination (Twomey et al., 2016; Stolk et al., 2013) have identified the signature, accumulate-to-bound neural activity characteristic of evidence accumulation in the sequential sampling process.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous EEG research.

claim: Previous findings show a centroparietal positivity (CPP) component in the event-related potential that rises with sensory evidence accumulation across time.
source: Specifically, these findings show a centropareital positivity (CPP) component in the event-related potential that rises with sensory evidence accumulation across time.
evidence: This is supported by previous research on CPP.

claim: In the isolated condition, the data replicated previous findings showing a clear CPP event-related potential whose slope of rise was strongly modulated by motion coherence (GLMM, p<0.001 and p=0.01 for study 1 and 2 respectively).
source: consistent with the previous literature, we found that in the isolated condition, our data replicated those earlier findings: Figure 4a shows a clear CPP event-related potential whose slope of rise was strongly modulated by motion coherence (GLMM, p<0.001 and p=0.01 for study 1 and 2 receptively, see Supplementary file 1d and Figure 4—figure supplement 2 for more details).
evidence: This is a statistical result from EEG data analysis shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Response-locked CPP waveforms converge to one another for high vs low coherence trials at the moment of the response.
source: Importantly, we have added the response-locked analysis of the CPP signals (see Figure 4—figure supplement 4). We do see that the response-locked CPP waveforms converge to one another for high vs low coherence trials at the moment of the response.
evidence: This is a result from response-locked EEG analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: The CPP slope was larger within every given coherence bin when the participant was paired with an HCA vs LCA (study 1 p=0.15, study 2 p<0.01).
source: We tested if the CPP slope were larger within every given coherence bin when the participant was paired with an HCA (vs LCA). Indeed, the data demonstrated a larger slope of CPP rise under HCA vs LCA (Figure 4c, study 1 for the social condition p=0.15 but for the second study p<0.01, see Tables 3 and 4 for more details).
evidence: This is a statistical result from EEG data analysis shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Interpersonal alignment of confidence is associated with a modulation of neural evidence accumulation by the social exchange of information.
source: These findings demonstrate that interpersonal alignment of confidence is associated with a modulation of neural evidence accumulation – as quantified by CPP – by the social exchange of information (also see Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the EEG data analysis.

claim: The study brought together two so-far-unrelated research directions: confidence in decision making under uncertainty and interpersonal alignment in communication.
source: We brought together two so-far-unrelated research directions: confidence in decision making under uncertainty and interpersonal alignment in communication.
evidence: This is a statement about the study's contribution.

claim: The study provides a model-based, theoretically grounded neural mechanism for going from individual, idiosyncratic representations of uncertainty to socially transmitted confidence expressions.
source: For decision science, we provide a model-based, theoretically grounded neural mechanism for going from individual, idiosyncratic representations of uncertainty (Navajas et al., 2017; Fleming et al., 2010) to socially transmitted confidence expressions (Bahrami et al., 2010; Bang et al., 2017) that are seamlessly shared and allow for successful cooperation.
evidence: This is a statement about the study's contribution to decision science.

claim: The social-to-neuronal coupling mechanism borrowed from the communication literature is crucial in understanding the neuronal basis of relationship between subjectively private and socially shared uncertainty.
source: The social-to-neuronal coupling mechanism that we borrowed from the communication literature (Hasson and Frith, 2016; Wheatley et al., 2019) is crucial in this new understanding of the neuronal basis of relationship between subjectively private and socially shared uncertainty.
evidence: This is an inference about the importance of the coupling mechanism.

claim: The study created a laboratory model in which the goal of communication was to arrive at a shared belief about uncertainty.
source: For communication science, by examining perceptual decision making under uncertainty in social context, we created a laboratory model in which the goal of communication was to arrive at a shared belief about uncertainty (rather than creating a look-up table for the meaning of actions [Stolk et al., 2016; Silbert et al., 2014; Honey et al., 2012]).
evidence: This is a statement about the study's contribution to communication science.

claim: A consensus emerging from brain-in-interaction works is that successful interpersonal alignment entails the mutual construction of a shared cognitive space between brains.
source: A consensus emerging from these works is that, at a conceptual level, successful interpersonal alignment entails the mutual construction of a shared cognitive space between brains (Stolk et al., 2015; Wheatley et al., 2019; Friston and Frith, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: A shared cognitive space would allow interacting brains to adjust their internal dynamics to converge on shared beliefs and meanings.
source: This would allow interacting brains to adjust their internal dynamics to converge on shared beliefs and meanings (Hasson and Frith, 2016; Gallotti and Frith, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Brain-to-brain interactions need to be described in terms of information flow to identify the neurobiological substrates of shared cognitive space.
source: To identify the neurobiological substrates of such shared cognitive space, brain-to-brain interactions need to be described in terms of information flow, i.e., the impact that interacting partners have on one another's brain dynamics (Wheatley et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Evidence for information flow has predominantly consisted of demonstrations of alignment of brain-to-brain activity when people process the same sensory input.
source: The evidence for such information flow has predominantly consisted of demonstrations of alignment of brain-to-brain activity (i.e. synchrony at macroscopic level, e.g. fMRI BOLD signal) when people process the same (simple or complex) sensory input (Honey et al., 2012; Hasson et al., 2004; Breveglieri et al., 2014; Mukamel et al., 2005; Hasson and Honey, 2012) or engage in complimentary communicative (Silbert et al., 2014) roles to achieve a common goal.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Dynamic coupling has been suggested as a more general description of the nature of brain-to-brain interaction.
source: More recently, dynamic coupling (rather than synchrony) has been suggested as a more general description of the nature of brain-to-brain interaction (Hasson and Frith, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: No computational framework grounded in the principles of neural computing has been offered that could propose a plausible quantitative mechanism for empirical observations of brain-to-brain coupling.
source: Going beyond the intuitive notions of synchrony and coupling, to our knowledge, no computational framework – grounded in the principles of neural computing – has been offered that could propose a plausible quantitative mechanism for these empirical observations of brain-to-brain coupling.
evidence: This identifies a gap in the literature based on the authors' review.

claim: Emergence of confidence matching showed that participants coordinated their decision confidence with their social partner.
source: Emergence of confidence matching (Figure 1b) showed that participants coordinated their decision confidence with their social partner.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the behavioral data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Pupil data suggested that participant's belief about uncertainty was shaped by the social coordination.
source: Pupil data (Figure 2) suggested that participant's belief about uncertainty was indeed shaped by the social coordination.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the pupillometry data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The neural attractor model drew predictions for behavior and neuronal activity that were born out by the data.
source: This model drew predictions for behavior (Figure 3d) and neuronal activity (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplements 1–5) that were born out by the data.
evidence: This is a statement about the model's predictive success.

claim: The overwhelming majority of previous works employing sequential sampling models to explain choice confidence have opted for the drift diffusion family of models.
source: Although numerous previous works have employed sequential sampling models to explain choice confidence, the overwhelming majority (Pouget et al., 2016; Aitchison et al., 2015; Hanks and Summerfield, 2017; Gold and Shadlen, 2007; Ruff and Fehr, 2014; Schall, 2019; Kiani et al., 2014; Sanders et al., 2016; Kiani and Shadlen, 2009; Krajbich and Rangel, 2011) have opted for the drift diffusion family of models.
evidence: This is an assessment of the literature supported by multiple citations.

claim: Neural attractor models have been rarely used to understand confidence.
source: Neural attractor models have so far been rarely used to understand confidence (Rolls et al., 2010; Atiya et al., 2019; Wang, 2002).
evidence: This is an assessment of the literature supported by citations.

claim: The attractor model used is a reduced version of the original biophysical neural circuit model for motion discrimination.
source: Our attractor model is a reduced version (Wong and Wang, 2006) of the original biophysical neural circuit model for motion discrimination (Wang, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the original models.

claim: The specific affordances of attractor models allowed implementing social context as a sustained, tonic top-down feedback to both accumulator mechanisms.
source: The specific affordances of attractor models allowed us to implement social context as a sustained, tonic top-down feedback to both accumulator mechanisms.
evidence: This is a statement about the modeling approach.

claim: The study chose different sets of coherence levels for the discovery (experiment 1) and replication (experiment 2).
source: We chose different sets of coherence levels for the discovery (experiment 1) and replication (experiment 2). This choice was made deliberately.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental design.

claim: In experiment 1, a very high coherence (51%) level was included to optimize the experimental design for demonstrating the CPP component in the EEG signal.
source: In experiment 1 we included a very high coherence (51%) level to optimize the experimental design for demonstrating the CPP component in the EEG signal.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental design rationale.

claim: In experiment 2, peri-threshold coherence levels were employed to focus on behavior around the perceptual threshold to strengthen the model fitting and model comparison.
source: In experiment 2, we employed peri-threshold coherence levels in order to focus on behavior around the perceptual threshold to strengthen the model fitting and model comparison.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental design rationale.

claim: The study did not directly examine neural alignment between interaction partners.
source: For example, our study did not directly examine neural alignment between interaction partners. We measured the EEG signal one participant at a time.
evidence: This is a statement about a limitation of the study.

claim: The participant interacted with an alleged (experimenter-controlled) partner in any given trial.
source: The participant interacted with an alleged (experimenter-controlled) partner in any given trial.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental design.

claim: Testing the hypotheses raised by the neural attractor model did not require hyper-scanning of two participants at the same time.
source: Moreover, while the hypotheses raised by our neural attractor model did examine the nature of brain dynamics involved in evidence accumulation under social context, testing these hypotheses did not require hyper-scanning of two participants at the same time.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental design rationale.

claim: Under joint conditions, the group choice is determined through the comparison of the choices and confidences of the partners.
source: For example, under joint conditions, the group choice is determined through the comparison of the choices and confidences of the partners.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental design.

claim: The participant has a more complex task of matching their response not only with their perceptual experience but also coordinating it with the partner to achieve the best possible outcome under joint conditions.
source: As a result, the participant has a more complex task of matching their response not only with their perceptual experience but also coordinating it with the partner to achieve the best possible outcome.
evidence: This is an inference about the task complexity.

claim: There is greater outcome uncertainty under joint vs individual conditions.
source: For the same reason, there is greater outcome uncertainty under joint vs individual conditions.
evidence: This is an inference about uncertainty in the task.

claim: Studies in perceptual decision making typically employ a small number of extensively trained participants (approximately 6–10 individuals).
source: Typically, studies in perceptual decision making employ a small number of extensively trained participants (approximately 6–10 individuals).
evidence: This is a statement about common practice in the field.

claim: Social neuroscience studies typically recruit larger samples (often more than 20 participants) without extensive training protocols.
source: Social neuroscience studies, on the other hand, recruit larger samples (often more than 20 participants) without extensive training protocols.
evidence: This is a statement about common practice in the field.

claim: Each participant underwent around 4000 training trials.
source: Note, for example, that each of our participants underwent around 4000 training trials.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental procedure.

claim: The initial study (N=12) yielded robust results that showed the hypothesized effects nearly completely.
source: Importantly, our initial study (N=12) yielded robust results that showed the hypothesized effects nearly completely, supporting the adequacy of our power estimate.
evidence: This is a statement about the results of study 1.

claim: The joint decisions were not an agreement between partners but were automatically assigned to the most confident choice.
source: For example, the joint decisions were not an agreement between partners (Bahrami et al., 2010; Bahrami et al., 2012). Instead, following a number of previous works (Bang et al., 2017; Bang et al., 2020), joint decisions were automatically assigned to the most confident choice.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental design.

claim: Partner's confidence and choice were random variables drawn from a distribution prespecified by the experimenter.
source: In addition, partner's confidence and choice were random variables drawn from a distribution prespecified by the experimenter and therefore, by design, unresponsive to the participant's behavior.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental design.

claim: The partner's response times and accuracy were not entirely random but matched carefully to the participant's behavior prerecorded in the individual session.
source: note however that the partner's response times and accuracy were not entirely random but matched carefully to the participant's behavior prerecorded in the individual session
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental design.

claim: A total of 27 participants were recruited for a two-session experiment – isolated and social session.
source: A total of 27 participants (12 in experiment 1 and 15 in experiment 2; 10 females; average age: 24 years; all naïve to the purpose of the experiment) were recruited for a two-session experiment – isolated and social session.
evidence: This is a statement about participant recruitment.

claim: All participants reported normal or corrected-to-normal vision.
source: All subjects reported normal or corrected-to-normal vision.
evidence: This is a statement about participant characteristics.

claim: The experiments were approved by the local Ethics Committee at Shaheed Rajaei University's Department of computer engineering.
source: The experiments were approved by the local Ethics Committee at Shaheed Rajaei University's Department of computer engineering.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

claim: After fixation for 300 ms was confirmed by closed-loop real-time eye tracking, two choice-target points appeared at 10° eccentricity.
source: In every trial (Figure 1a), after fixation for 300 ms was confirmed by closed-loop real-time eye tracking, two choice-target points appeared at 10° eccentricity corresponding to the two possible motion directions (left and right).
evidence: This describes the trial structure.

claim: A dynamic RDM was centrally displayed for 500 ms in a virtual aperture (5° diameter) after a short random delay (200–500 ms, truncated exponential distribution).
source: After a short random delay (200–500 ms, truncated exponential distribution), a dynamic RDM (see Shadlen and Newsome, 2001) was centrally displayed for 500 ms in a virtual aperture (5° diameter).
evidence: This describes the stimulus presentation.

claim: RT was calculated as the time between the onset of the motion stimulus sequence and the onset of deviation of the mouse pointer at the end of stimulus presentation.
source: RT was calculated as the time between the onset of the motion stimulus sequence and the onset of deviation of the mouse pointer (see Materials and methods for more details) (Resulaj et al., 2009) at the end of stimulus presentation.
evidence: This describes the RT measurement method.

claim: Participants were instructed to try to maximize the joint accuracy of their social decisions.
source: Participants were instructed to try to maximize the joint accuracy of their social decisions.
evidence: This describes the task instructions.

claim: For each block the participants were led to believe that they were paired with a new, anonymous human partner.
source: Following from an earlier study (Bang et al., 2017), for each block the participants were led to believe that they were paired with a new, anonymous human partner.
evidence: This describes the experimental deception.

claim: In reality, participants were paired with four computer generated partners constructed and tuned to parameters obtained from the participant's own behavior in the isolated session.
source: In reality, in separate blocks, they were paired with four computer generated partners (henceforward, CGPs; see Materials and methods) constructed and tuned to parameters obtained from the participant's own behavior in the isolated session
evidence: This describes the actual experimental design.

claim: For study 2, two CGPs (HCA and LCA) were used while the agent accuracy was similar to those of participants.
source: For study 2, we used two CGPs (HCA and LCA) while the agent accuracy was similar to those of participants (Bang and Fleming, 2018) (Wilcoxon rank sum, p=0.37, df = 29, zval = 0.89).
evidence: This describes the CGP design for study 2.

claim: Questionnaire results confirmed that the manipulation worked and none of the subjects suspected their partners was an artificial one.
source: Our questionnaire results also confirmed that our manipulation indeed worked (Figure 1—figure supplement 4) and more importantly none of the subject suspected their partners was an artificial one.
evidence: This is a result from post-experiment questionnaires shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: A permutation analysis confirmed that confidence matching did not arise trivially from mere pairing with any random partner.
source: Having observed the confidence matching effect in both studies (Figure 1b), a permutation analysis confirmed that this effect did not arise trivially from mere pairing with any random partner (Bang et al., 2017; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a result from permutation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The difference between the participant's confidence and that of their partner was smaller in the social (vs isolated) condition.
source: The difference between the participant's confidence and that of their partner was smaller in the social (vs isolated) condition (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) consistent with the prediction that participants would match their average confidence to that of their partner in the social session (Bang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a result from the analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.
